blocks.text: 1. Object Detection

blocks.alt: An input image goes through a detector to produce boxes and labels

blocks.text: Image Classification, the previous topic, assigned a single label to an entire image, saying nothing about location. Object Detection addresses exactly that limitation by locating individual objects, explored throughout this topic.
It predicts both what an object is and where it is, for every object in an image, a genuinely richer, more complete task covered throughout the rest of this topic.
2. Recapping The Gap Being Closed

This connects back to the genuine limitation of Image Classification, already covered in the previous topic. Image Classification genuinely says nothing about where within the image an object actually is.
Object Detection genuinely closes that exact gap, directly building on everything already covered throughout Image Classification while adding the missing spatial dimension.
3. The Bounding Box Concept

blocks.alt: An object is described by bounding box coordinates

blocks.text: The genuinely core output format is a bounding box: a rectangle marking exactly where an object sits within the image, a genuinely simple, direct way to represent object location.
It is genuinely defined by its position and size, wrapping tightly around the detected object, giving Object Detection a genuinely concrete, structured output beyond just a single class label.

blocks.text: 4. Two Problems Solved At Once

blocks.alt: Object detection answers both what is it and where is it

blocks.text: This connects back to Image Classification's own single-label output, already covered. Object Detection genuinely solves two problems simultaneously: classification, already covered, and localization, already covered in this topic.

This is a genuinely harder task than Image Classification's own single-label prediction, already covered, since the network must now genuinely produce both a label and a precise spatial location together.
5. Multiple Objects Per Image

blocks.alt: Image classification gives one label while object detection gives many boxes

blocks.text: This connects back to the single-label assumption, already covered in Image Classification. Object Detection genuinely drops that assumption entirely, a genuinely important structural difference between these two tasks.

A single image can genuinely contain many objects, each with its own genuinely separate bounding box and label, a genuinely realistic scenario that plain Image Classification, already covered, could never properly represent.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This ability to detect multiple objects per image, already covered in this topic, is exactly why Object Detection is considerably more computationally involved than Image Classification, already covered as the foundational, simpler task.

blocks.text: 6. Confidence Scores

blocks.alt: A predicted box carries a confidence score

blocks.text: This connects back to Softmax probabilities, already covered in Image Classification. Each detected bounding box genuinely comes with its own confidence score, a genuinely direct extension of that earlier probability-based idea.
This score reflects how genuinely certain the network is that a real object actually exists there, letting downstream applications genuinely filter out low-confidence, likely spurious detections.
7. A Preview Of Non-Max Suppression

blocks.alt: Overlapping boxes are reduced by non-max suppression to one box per object

blocks.text: A genuinely common, real practical problem follows. A single genuine object can genuinely trigger several overlapping, redundant bounding box predictions, rather than just one clean detection.

A technique called Non-Max Suppression, covered further in this course, genuinely cleans this up, keeping only the genuinely best, most confident box among a cluster of overlapping, redundant predictions.
8. A Preview Of Intersection Over Union

blocks.alt: A predicted box is compared against a ground truth box via IoU

blocks.text: A genuinely important, related evaluation concept connects back to Evaluation Metrics, already covered in its own module. Measuring how well a predicted bounding box genuinely overlaps with the true one is covered further later in this course.
This genuinely important, related idea will directly build on the bounding box concept already covered earlier in this topic, providing a genuinely precise way to judge detection quality.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Object Detection Is Genuinely Necessary
This connects back to needing to know where objects are, not just what they are. Object Detection, already covered in this topic, directly provides both pieces of information together.

Real-world applications like self-driving vehicles or security systems are another genuine case; these genuinely require locating multiple objects simultaneously, exactly what Object Detection, already covered, provides.
10. Worked Example

The example below directly demonstrates a genuinely simplified Object Detection output, listing several detected bounding boxes with their own class labels and confidence scores, illustrating the concepts already covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
detections = [
    {"class": "car", "box": (50, 60, 200, 180), "confidence": 0.94},   # already covered as a bounding box in this topic
    {"class": "person", "box": (220, 90, 280, 240), "confidence": 0.88},
    {"class": "car", "box": (55, 62, 205, 185), "confidence": 0.71},   # a genuinely redundant, overlapping detection
    {"class": "dog", "box": (300, 200, 360, 260), "confidence": 0.65},
]

confidence_threshold = 0.7  # already covered as filtering low-confidence detections in this topic

filtered_detections = [d for d in detections if d["confidence"] >= confidence_threshold]

print(f"Total raw detections: {len(detections)}")
print(f"Detections above confidence threshold {confidence_threshold}: {len(filtered_detections)}")
for d in filtered_detections:
    print(f"  {d['class']} at {d['box']}, confidence {d['confidence']:.2f}")

print("\nNotice the two overlapping 'car' detections, already covered as the motivation for Non-Max Suppression in this topic")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows a low-confidence detection filtered out, and two genuinely overlapping car detections still present, exactly the redundancy problem already covered in this topic as the motivation for Non-Max Suppression.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Object Detection predicts both what an object is and where it is, for every object in an image.
It closes the gap left by Image Classification, which says nothing about object location.
A bounding box is a rectangle marking an object's position and size within the image.
It solves two problems at once: classification and localization.
It drops the single-label assumption, since a single image can contain many objects.
Each detected bounding box comes with its own confidence score.
Non-Max Suppression cleans up redundant, overlapping detections of the same object.
Intersection over Union measures how well a predicted box overlaps with the true object location.
Next up: Semantic Segmentation, which pushes localization even further, down to the individual pixel.
